nodes.name: Game Development - Level Design
principles: Visual guidance leads the player through space using signifiers, affordances, and signal-to-noise ratio
Critical areas should be information-rich; less critical areas should be simplified or blurred
Use perspective lines to create natural sightlines toward objectives
Rhythm disruption (breaking a pattern) draws attention more effectively than adding detail
Dynamic range in saturation/brightness makes important elements stand out
Spatial transformations (narrow corridor to open space) capture attention
Signifiers should be used sparingly — immersion breaks when players feel they are following arrows rather than making decisions

nodes.name: Game Development - Lighting for Games
principles: Key light establishes the primary illumination direction and mood
Fill light softens shadows from key, controlling contrast ratio
Rim/back light separates subject from background by creating edge highlights
Practical lights (lamps, screens) provide motivated lighting within the scene
Color temperature creates emotional tone: warm (3200K) = safe/comfortable; cool (6500K+) = sterile/dangerous
Dynamic range in lighting (bright highlights against dark shadows) creates drama and visual interest
Light should guide the eye — brightest areas draw attention first

nodes.name: Game Development - Environment Art
principles: Modular design enables building vast worlds from reusable components
PBR materials (Physically Based Rendering) ensure consistent appearance under any lighting
Trim sheets and tiling textures reduce asset count while maintaining visual variety
Scale cues (door frames, handrails, furniture) establish believable proportions
Surface detail hierarchy: macro shapes read at distance, micro details up close
Environmental wear tells history — scorch marks, rust, fading paint suggest past events

nodes.name: Game Development - Visual Storytelling
principles: Every object placement implies intent — what was left behind? What was moved?
Signs of habitation (chairs pushed in, food on table) suggest recent presence
Damage and decay tell temporal stories — fresh vs. ancient environments feel different
Color palettes communicate faction identity and emotional state
Lighting quality reveals narrative tone: harsh = conflict; soft = safety
Environmental clutter density correlates with activity level of the space

nodes.name: Game Development - Game Feel
principles: Juice (screen shake, particles, sound) communicates impact and weight
Feedback must be immediate — player action to response within 100ms feels responsive
Particle effects communicate state changes: hit sparks, shield impacts, explosion debris
Sound design layers frequency bands: low = power/tension; high = alertness/beauty
Camera movement reinforces physics — slow-mo on impact, snap-back to normal
Visual feedback should match audio feedback for cohesive sensory experience

nodes.name: Art School - Color Theory
principles: Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) advance visually; cool colors (blue, green, purple) recede
Complementary color pairs (opposite on wheel) create maximum contrast and visual tension
Analogous colors (adjacent on wheel) create harmony and calm
Color temperature contrast (warm vs. cool) is more emotionally powerful than value contrast alone
Saturation reduction in background elements pushes them back; high saturation pulls forward
Color associations are cultural but some are universal: red=danger/passion, blue=calm/distance, green=nature/safety
A limited palette (3-5 colors) creates cohesion; unlimited palettes feel chaotic

nodes.name: Art School - Composition
principles: Rule of thirds: placing subjects at intersection points creates dynamic balance
Golden ratio (1.618) appears naturally in pleasing compositions — use as guide, not rule
Leading lines draw the eye through the composition toward a focal point
Framing within framing (arches, windows, debris fields) adds depth and focus
Balance can be symmetrical (formal, stable) or asymmetrical (dynamic, interesting)
Negative space is as important as positive space — it gives the eye rest
Triangular composition creates stability; diagonal composition creates tension

nodes.name: Art School - Form and Mass
principles: Silhouette readability determines if a shape reads at distance — test by filling with solid black
Geometric simplicity (box, sphere, cylinder) communicates function clearly
Proportion changes perception: tall=noble/imposing; short=stable/grounded; wide=powerful
Industrial design follows form-function relationship: visible structure implies purpose
Edge variation (hard vs. soft edges) creates visual interest and guides attention
Repetition with variation creates rhythm without monotony
Scale contrast (large small element among small elements) draws immediate attention

nodes.name: Art School - Light and Shadow
principles: Chiaroscuro (strong light-dark contrast) creates drama and volume
Rim lighting separates subjects from background by creating edge definition
Shadow direction establishes light source consistency — inconsistent shadows break believability
Soft shadows = large/diffuse light source; hard shadows = small/distant light source
Light falloff (inverse square law) creates depth perception in 3D space
Cast shadows ground objects to surfaces — floating without shadow feels disconnected
Ambient occlusion at contact points adds weight and realism

nodes.name: Art School - Material Rendering
principles: Roughness controls how light scatters: smooth=specular highlights; rough=diffuse reflection
Metallic property determines if surface reflects environment (metal) or has base color (non-metal)
Surface imperfections sell realism: scratches, fingerprints, wear patterns break up perfect surfaces
Normal maps add micro-detail without geometry cost — essential for game performance
Subsurface scattering makes translucent materials (skin, wax, fabric) feel alive
Material aging follows predictable patterns: rust at edges, fading on exposed surfaces, grime in crevices
PBR workflow ensures materials look consistent under any lighting condition

nodes.name: School_3_Film_School - Cinematography
principles: Camera angle defines power relationship: low angle = subject powerful; high angle = subject vulnerable
Close-up creates intimacy and emotional connection; wide shot establishes context and scale
Dutch angle (tilted camera) creates unease and disorientation
Tracking shots follow action and create immersion; static shots create tension and anticipation
Depth of field isolates subjects - shallow DOF for emotion, deep DOF for environmental storytelling
Camera movement should be motivated by narrative purpose, not decoration

nodes.name: School_3_Film_School - Lighting for Film
principles: Three-point lighting: key (main), fill (soften shadows), rim (separate from background)
Motivated lighting: every light source should have a visible or implied practical source in the scene
High-key lighting (bright, low contrast) = comedy/safety; low-key lighting (dark, high contrast) = drama/tension
Practical lights (lamps, screens, fire) provide both illumination and narrative context
Color temperature shifts between scenes signal emotional transitions

nodes.name: School_3_Film_School - Production Design
principles: Every prop placement tells a story - what was left in hurry vs. careful arrangement
Period accuracy creates believability but should serve the narrative, not constrain it
Color palette consistency across sets establishes visual identity for locations
Scale and proportion communicate function: control panels at waist height, warning lights at eye level
Signs of use (wear patterns, personal items) make spaces feel inhabited rather than staged

nodes.name: School_4_Architecture_School - Spatial Design
principles: Human scale reference: door heights ~2m, ceiling heights 2.4-3.5m for comfort
Circulation paths should be intuitive - main corridors wider than secondary passages
Room size relative to function: intimate spaces <20sqm, gathering spaces >50sqm
Thresholds (doorways, arches) signal transition between spatial experiences
Sight lines through spaces create depth and guide movement naturally

nodes.name: School_4_Architecture_School - Materiality
principles: Material honesty: surfaces should express their true nature - concrete looks like concrete
Texture contrast adds visual interest at human touch distance (0.5-2m from viewer)
Floor materials define function: hard = utilitarian; soft = comfort/rest areas
Wall treatments communicate permanence: metal/concrete = permanent; fabric/wood = temporary

nodes.name: School_4_Architecture_School - Lighting Design
principles: Layered lighting: ambient (general), task (functional), accent (dramatic)
Task lighting focused on work surfaces at 300-500 lux; ambient at 100-200 lux
Accent lighting creates focal points and visual hierarchy within spaces
Natural light simulation through directional sources with warm color temperature

nodes.name: School_5_Engineering_School - Spacecraft Design
principles: Form follows physics: spacecraft shapes driven by aerodynamics (atmosphere) or volume efficiency (space)
Modular design enables repair and replacement - ISS modules bolt together like LEGO
Thermal management dictates external features: radiators, heat shields, reflective surfaces
Radiation shielding adds mass - often water walls or polyethylene composites in real designs
Solar arrays are large flat panels optimized for surface area - primary power source in space
Redundancy is built into critical systems - visible as duplicate components and access panels

nodes.name: School_5_Engineering_School - Industrial Design
principles: Ergonomic controls placed within natural reach zone (arm length, waist to shoulder height)
Control layout follows functional grouping: related functions clustered together
Status indicators at eye level; critical warnings in red/orange with high contrast
Cable management and clean surfaces reduce maintenance complexity and visual clutter

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Editor Modes
principles: Modeling Mode enables direct mesh creation and editing within the editor viewport
Mesh Paint Mode allows vertex color painting and material weight adjustment on static meshes
Foliage Mode enables rapid placement of vegetation with density, rotation, and scale variation controls
Viewport camera can be controlled via console commands for precise framing and composition

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Console Commands
principles: EditorModeManager ActivateMode command switches editor modes programmatically
ExecuteCommand allows running any Unreal Engine console command from external tools
Set_camera and set_viewport_camera enable cinematic camera positioning for screenshots
Screenshot command captures viewport images for LM Studio visual verification

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - MCP Geometry Tools
principles: control_actor spawn_actor creates actors in the world with specified transforms
add_component attaches StaticMeshComponents to actors for geometry placement
set_transform controls position, rotation, and scale of spawned actors precisely
manage_asset create/import handles asset creation and file import workflows

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Basic Shape Creation
principles: Primitive shapes (box, sphere, cylinder, cone) serve as foundation geometry for complex meshes
Scale and transform primitives creates varied proportions while maintaining clean topology
Multiple primitives combined via boolean operations create complex architectural forms
Grid snapping ensures consistent placement and modular alignment

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Sculpting Workflow
principles: Sculpt brushes (grab, pinch, smooth) enable organic shape manipulation on mesh surfaces
Brush size and strength control the scale and subtlety of sculpted details
Layer-based sculpting preserves non-destructive editing capability
Decimation reduces polygon count while preserving sculpted silhouette for game optimization

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Material Application
principles: Materials assigned to geometry via material slots in static mesh editor
PBR material parameters (roughness, metallic, base color) control surface appearance
Material instances allow variation without duplicating full material graphs
UV mapping ensures textures project correctly onto geometry surfaces

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Spatial Composition
principles: Objects compose in three dimensions - position relative to origin, neighbors, and sight lines matter
Balance achieved through mass distribution: heavy objects low and centered; light objects high and offset
Object placement creates visual paths that guide the eye through 3D space
Depth perception enhanced by overlapping elements and atmospheric perspective (fog distance)

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Grid Systems
principles: Modular grid (typically 64cm/2ft increments) enables consistent architectural composition
Grid snapping ensures props align with structural elements for believable placement
Multiple grid layers (structural, furnishing, clutter) create organized complexity
Consistent grid usage across all assets enables seamless modular assembly

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Distance and Scale
principles: Human-scale references establish believable proportions: door ~2m, chair ~0.9m, table ~0.75m
Corridor width 1.2-1.5m for single person; 2-3m for two-person passage
Ceiling height 2.4m (intimate) to 4m (grand) affects emotional perception of space
Debris density correlates with narrative: sparse = abandoned; dense = active/chaotic

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Spatial Relationships
principles: Every object should have a reason for its position relative to other elements
Light placement follows functional logic: work areas lit, corridors dimmer, corners darkest
Occlusion relationships create depth: foreground objects partially block background
The graph records spatial context - query it before placing any new element

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Michelangelo Procedure
principles: Rough-cut the form first: establish large shapes and proportions before details
Refine second pass: adjust relationships between elements and improve proportions
Detail third pass: add surface texture, wear patterns, and small props
Polish final pass: lighting adjustments, color correction, atmospheric effects
Each pass removes less but makes more difference - diminishing returns increase with each iteration

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Iteration Principles
principles: Start with biggest, most obvious elements first (walls, floors, major props)
Verify against reference before moving to details - catch errors early when cheap to fix
Each pass should be smaller and more precise than the last
Stop when further changes do not improve LM Studio assessment score

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Knowing When to Stop
principles: Goal is not exact match but capturing essence: feeling, principles, truth of the reference
If 10 iterations produce no improvement, return to research for new references or principles
Human feedback overrides objective analysis - if human says it feels wrong, it is wrong

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Failure Protocol
principles: After 10 failed iterations: return to research, find new references
Return to education: identify missing fundamental principle
Ask the human: show reference and best attempt, ask what they see that is different
Never iterate randomly - every change driven by specific observation or principle

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Lighting
principles: Lonely = single light source + cool temperature (4500K+) + high contrast shadows
Safe = multiple warm sources (3200K) + soft shadows + low contrast
Danger = flickering light + harsh shadows + scorched material palette
Awe = bright directional light (5500K) + dramatic shadows + rich detail surfaces
Mystery = dim colored lighting + deep shadows + obscured materials
Hope = single warm light source in darkness + high contrast worn-but-cared-for materials

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Materials
principles: Rough surfaces = rustic/old/dangerous feeling; smooth surfaces = clean/new/safe
Warm materials (wood, fabric) = comfort and intimacy
Cold materials (metal, glass) = sterile or imposing depending on context
Worn but maintained surfaces suggest hope and resilience in harsh environments

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Sound
principles: Low frequencies create tension, power, dread - use for danger and awe scenes
High frequencies create alertness, anxiety, beauty - use for mystery and hope
Silence creates loneliness, peace, or terror depending on visual context
Steady ambient hum = safety and normalcy; irregular sounds = tension and uncertainty

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Space
principles: Low ceilings (2.4m) = oppressive/intimate/cozy depending on lighting quality
High ceilings (4m+) = freedom/awe or isolation depending on content
Narrow corridors create tension; open spaces create safety or vulnerability
Threshold transitions (narrow to wide) amplify emotional impact of revealed space

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Organization System
principles: Every reference gets unique ID, source URL, date collected, category, subject, emotional tags
Store in Graphify as Reference nodes linked to Pattern nodes and Education nodes
Folder structure: research/[category]/[subject]/ with images, descriptions, extracted parameters

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Avoiding Duplication
principles: Before new research, query Graphify for existing patterns on same subject
If patterns exist, start from those - only research new aspects
Never re-research the same thing unless previous research failed verification

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Cross-Referencing
principles: Study related domains: naval ship lighting informs station lighting; hospital lighting informs habitat lighting
Link related references across categories - graph shows connections humans miss
Principles transfer across domains: same composition rules apply to space stations and cathedrals

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Reference Decay
principles: References age - patterns extracted months ago may be superseded by better understanding
Periodically re-verify old patterns against new references
Mark patterns as superseded rather than deleting them - history matters for learning

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Combinatorial Creativity
principles: Nothing is truly original - everything is a remix of existing references
The art is in which references you combine and how you transform them
Combine principles from unrelated domains: Gothic cathedral architecture + zero-G physics

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Extrapolation
principles: Take a principle from one domain and apply it to another unexpectedly
Ask what-if questions: what if a space station had cathedral proportions?
Extrapolate real-world constraints into future contexts with imagination

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Constraints as Creativity
principles: DSL defines constraints - these are not limitations but the frame that makes painting possible
Engine limits (polygon count, draw calls) force creative optimization solutions
Creative constraints produce more focused and intentional design decisions

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Idea Log
principles: Save ideas that do not fit current task as Idea nodes in Graphify
Ideas can be combined later - the graph grows with what could be, not just what is
Review idea log periodically for unexpected connections and opportunities

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Presenting Options
principles: When multiple approaches exist, present them clearly to the human with pros/cons
Never assume you know what the human wants - show options and let them choose
Visual comparisons (screenshots) are more effective than textual descriptions

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Asking for Guidance
principles: When stuck after multiple iterations, ask directly: I have tried X, Y, Z. Do you see something missing?
The human sees things the AI does not - they hold the vision
Frame questions specifically: what emotion is wrong? what proportion feels off?

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Incorporating Feedback
principles: Record all human feedback in Graphify and link to relevant patterns
Human feedback overrides objective analysis when conflicts arise
If LM Studio says it matches but human says it feels wrong - the human is right. Research why.

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Mirror Protocol
principles: Job is to reflect the human vision back with clarity, not impose own aesthetic
Show work honestly and ask if it matches what they imagined
If it does not match, that is not failure - it is the next iteration. The mirror gets clearer each reflection.

nodes.name: School_13_Record_Education - Complete Education Record
principles: All principles from all schools should be linked to relevant Feature Ledger entries
Cross-reference related principles across disciplines for richer understanding
Education is never complete - new references and insights continuously enrich the graph
The tree grows with every lesson. The mirror sharpens with every insight.

nodes.name: Player_Character_Model - Research Principle 3

nodes.name: Player_Character_Model - Research Principle 4

nodes.name: Player_Character_Suit - Research Principle 8

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Lunar regolith grain size: fine dust <1mm (lunar dust), up to 1cm (soil particles)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Regolith density: ~1.5 g/cm3, increases with depth due to compaction
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Color palette: gray-brown base (#8B7D6B) with subtle orange/green glass beads at volcanic deposits
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Surface texture: sharp angular particles (not rounded like Earth sand) — creates high micro-roughness
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: PBR Base Color: R=139 G=125 B=107 (warm gray), variation ±15% across surface for natural look
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: PBR Roughness: 0.85-0.95 (very rough — no smooth surfaces in unconsolidated regolith)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 7
nodes.content: PBR Metallic: 0.05-0.1 (trace elemental iron from solar wind, but mostly non-metallic)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: Normal map detail: high-frequency angular particle edges at 0.1mm scale, medium-scale impact craters at 1-10cm
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Surface - Research Principle 10

nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Surface

nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Particles

nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Particles

nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Particles

nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Particles

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Particles - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: In sunlight: particles appear bright white-gray with specular highlights on glassy surfaces

nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Particles

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Particles - Research Principle 9

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Bootprint depth in regolith: ~2-3cm for astronaut weight (~80kg with suit) on firm surface
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Footprints

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Edge detail: sharp, well-defined walls — angular particles lock together (unlike Earth sand)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Footprints

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Footprints persist indefinitely — no wind/water erosion on Moon, only micrometeorite gardening
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Footprints

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Deformation pattern: material displaced laterally and upward at edges, creating raised rim
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Footprints

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: Pressure required to compact regolith: ~10-20 kPa for initial penetration, increases with depth

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: Boot sole pattern transfers clearly — Apollo suits had hexagonal tread for traction
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Footprints

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 7
nodes.content: Footprint fill-in time: effectively infinite (no atmosphere), but gradual settling from seismic vibrations
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Footprints

nodes.name: Ground_Sand_Footprints - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: In game context: footprints should persist for extended duration, slowly fade over minutes not seconds
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Sand_Footprints

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Rock types in regolith: anorthositic (highlands), basaltic (mare), with plagioclase, olivine, augite minerals
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Color variation: gray-white anorthosite (#C8BFB0) vs dark basalt (#4A4540) — 20-30% color variation
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Fracture patterns: angular blocky fractures from impact brecciation, not tectonic folding
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Surface weathering: space weathering creates darkening (radiation exposure), maturation index correlates with darkness
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: PBR Base Color: R=100 G=95 B=88 (weathered gray), with darker veins of basaltic material
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: PBR Roughness: 0.7-0.9 (fractured surfaces, not polished)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 7
nodes.content: PBR Metallic: 0.02 (mostly silicate minerals, minimal metallic content)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: Scale cues: rocks range from dust grains to boulders >1m, most common size 1-10cm fragments
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Rock_Surface - Research Principle 9
nodes.content: Impact breccia texture: welded fragments in glassy matrix from meteorite impacts
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Rock_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Spacecraft hull materials: aluminum alloys (2219, 7075), titanium, gold foil MLI insulation
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Surface finish: brushed aluminum (#B8B0A8) with directional grain, anodized surfaces matte gray
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Wear patterns: scuff marks from tool contact, thermal cycling discoloration (blue/purple heat tint)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Corrosion: minimal in vacuum but atomic oxygen erosion on orbital surfaces creates dulling
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: PBR Base Color: R=184 G=176 B=168 (brushed aluminum), gold foil accents R=212 G=175 B=55
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: PBR Roughness: 0.3-0.5 for brushed surfaces, 0.1-0.2 for polished panels
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 7
nodes.content: PBR Metallic: 0.9-1.0 (highly reflective metal), with environment reflection intensity at 0.8
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: Reflectivity: specular highlights sharp and bright, reflections show high contrast due to no atmosphere
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Ground_Metal_Surface - Research Principle 9
nodes.content: Thermal protection: black carbon-composite heat shields (#2A2520) on reentry surfaces
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Ground_Metal_Surface

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Camera distance (third-person): 1.5-2.5m behind player, adjustable 0.8-4.0m range
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: FOV: 60-90 degrees default, wider for open spaces (90), narrower for tight corridors (60)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Mouse sensitivity curve: exponential with base 1.5, max rotation ~360deg/sec at highest setting
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Smoothing: camera lag 0.05-0.1s for cinematic feel, disabled during combat for responsiveness
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: Collision detection: raycast from camera to player, prevent clipping through geometry
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: Look constraints: pitch -60 to +80 degrees (can look down at feet, up at sky), yaw 360 unrestricted
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 7
nodes.content: Visual guidance application: signal-to-noise ratio — important objects have higher contrast/saturation
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Look - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: Instinct elements: player attention drawn to faces, movement, and light sources automatically
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Look

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Walk cycle duration: 1.2s per full cycle (0.6s per leg), ~85 steps/min at normal pace
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Stride length: 0.7-0.9m for average human, reduced to 0.4-0.5m in bulky EVA suit
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Step height: heel clearance 2-3cm above ground, increased to 5cm on uneven terrain
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: IK foot placement: ankle roll compensation ±15 degrees for slope adaptation
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: Terrain adaptation: step length reduces by 30% on loose/granular surfaces (sand/regolith)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: Foot contact sound: sharp crunch in regolith (angular particles), softer thud on metal
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 7
nodes.content: Weight distribution: 60% heel strike, gradual roll to toe-off over 40% of stance phase
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Step - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: Suit restriction effects: reduced arm swing amplitude by 30%, slight forward lean from PLSS weight
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Step

nodes.name: Verb_Bend - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Bending posture: knee flexion 60-90 degrees, torso leans forward ~45 degrees
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Bend

nodes.name: Verb_Bend - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Center of gravity shift: moves downward and forward during bend, requires balance adjustment
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Bend

nodes.name: Verb_Bend - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Suit articulation limits: knee bellows allow full flexion but elbow joints resist deep bends
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Bend

nodes.name: Verb_Bend - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Bend duration: 0.8s to reach full crouch position, 0.5s to return to standing
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Bend

nodes.name: Verb_Bend - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: Grip height at full bend: hands reach ~0.3m above ground for picking up objects
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Bend

nodes.name: Verb_Bend - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: Balance recovery: brief pause (0.2s) after standing from deep bend to re-stabilize
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Bend

nodes.name: Verb_PickUp - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Pickup animation chain: approach (1m) -> bend (0.8s) -> grasp (0.3s) -> rise (0.5s)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_PickUp

nodes.name: Verb_PickUp - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Grasp mechanics: three-finger pinch grip for small objects, power grip for tools
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_PickUp

nodes.name: Verb_PickUp - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Object weight perception: visual sag in arm for heavy items (>5kg), subtle animation variation
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_PickUp

nodes.name: Verb_PickUp - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Suit glove limitation: reduced precision grip due to thick gloves, larger objects easier to grasp
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_PickUp

nodes.name: Verb_PickUp - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: Pickup sound: sharp regolith crunch when lifting from surface, metallic clank on hard surfaces
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_PickUp

nodes.name: Verb_Drop - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Drop animation: arm extends forward, hand opens, object falls with gravity (1.62 m/s2 lunar)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Drop

nodes.name: Verb_Drop - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Object bounce in regolith: minimal bounce (<2cm) due to granular energy absorption
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Drop

nodes.name: Verb_Drop - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Object bounce on metal: high bounce (10-30cm) depending on drop height and material elasticity
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Drop

nodes.name: Verb_Drop - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Dust cloud on impact: small particle burst visible when dropping into loose regolith
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Drop

nodes.name: Verb_Drop - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: Sound design: dull thud in sand, sharp metallic ring on hard surfaces, duration 0.2-0.5s
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Drop

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 1
nodes.content: Shovel blade angle: 30-45 degrees to surface for optimal penetration in regolith
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 2
nodes.content: Force application: downward thrust ~50N at blade edge, forward pull ~30N to lift material
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 3
nodes.content: Material displacement: scoop volume ~2-3 liters per shovel load (standard astronaut tool)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 4
nodes.content: Regolith behavior: angular particles flow like dry granular material, no cohesion (unlike wet Earth sand)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 5
nodes.content: Animation chain: approach -> thrust blade (0.4s) -> lift with material (0.5s) -> dump (0.3s)
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 6
nodes.content: Sound layers: blade penetration crunch (low-mid freq), material cascade (high freq rustle), impact thud
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 7
nodes.content: Particle effects: small regolith cloud on blade entry, trailing particles during swing arc
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.name: Verb_Shovel - Research Principle 8
nodes.content: Suit restriction: full arm extension limited by elbow joint, maximum scoop depth ~30cm below surface
nodes.source: NASA Apollo References / Lunar Regolith Science / Game Design Research
nodes.subject: Verb_Shovel

nodes.source_evidence: Playtest shows players complete runs without realizing they achieved the 'costless life' bad ending (safe, complete, unreceived).
nodes.dsl_bible_source: The discovery this law produced — the failure ending: it is possible to finish a run having risked everything and protected nothing at cost. ... parameters.mask_shader_stage_node: PixelNormalWS (per-pixel), NOT VertexNormalWS, must drive a dust mask output. Epic UE5.8 official docs: VertexNormalWS 'can only be used in material inputs that are executed in the vertex shader, like WorldPositionOffset.'
parameters.noise_algorithm: Improved/gradient Perlin noise (Ken Perlin's 2002 correction), GPU-evaluated per-pixel via permutation/gradient texture lookups; ~50 pixel-shader instructions per Simon Green's reference implementation (GPU Gems 2 Ch.26).
parameters.crevice_curvature_technique: Raw per-vertex VertexNormal CANNOT resolve curvature/crevice detail; requires multi-sample normal-MAP texture reads (FWVN-style filter-width function), not single-sample vertex data.
parameters.material_cpp_constants_uncited: AccumulationRate=0.5, DecayRate=0.2, NormalThreshold=0.7 in the already-generated DustAccumulationMaterial.cpp trace to NO source found in this research -- flagged, not verified; needs citation or an in-engine art-tuning pass.
parameters.accumulation_shader_cost_instructions: ~240 instructions (built-in PerturbNormalHQ world-space bump path) vs ~412 instructions (custom multi-sample noise path) -- single practitioner data point.

acceptance_criteria: 1. DustAccumulationMaterial's mask output is driven by PixelNormalWS, not VertexNormalWS -- verify via material graph node inspection (MCP manage_asset) that no VertexNormalWS node feeds a pixel-shader-executed input (Opacity/BaseColor/mask channel).
2. Mask uses a GPU-evaluated gradient/Perlin-family noise (Material Editor Noise expression set to Perlin/Gradient, or an equivalent function) -- verify via material graph node inspection.
3. AccumulationRate/DecayRate/NormalThreshold constants (currently 0.5/0.2/0.7, uncited) are replaced with a cited value or an explicit in-engine art-tuning pass with screenshot evidence.
4. Dust mask color output matches Ground_Sand_Particles' verified #8B7D6B (RGB 139,125,107) -- verify via material parameter read-back or screenshot color sample.
5. Any crevice/curvature accumulation uses multi-sample normal-map-based curvature detection (e.g. FWVN-style), not raw VertexNormal alone -- verify via material graph inspection.

6. Mask visibly concentrates on horizontal/downward-facing and crevice surfaces vs. upward-facing surfaces in a PIE screenshot (vision tertiary), consistent with lunar dust-settling physics already established for Ground_Sand_Particles (discovery_6de7628185c32c90).
failure_sources: VertexNormalWS wired into a pixel-shader-stage material input (e.g. a mask/Opacity output) does not work -- Epic's official UE5.8 docs restrict VertexNormalWS to vertex-shader-executed inputs like WorldPositionOffset ONLY (dev.epicgames.com/documentation/unreal-engine/vector-material-expressions-in-unreal-engine, verified 2026-07-07). A real Epic Dev Community forum thread documents a developer hitting exactly this class of vertex/pixel-stage node confusion (forums.unrealengine.com/t/vertexnormalws-works-but-pixelnormalws-doesnt-why/764357).

Raw per-vertex VertexNormal data cannot produce good curvature/crevice detection for dirt/dust-in-cracks masking -- per the FWVN material-function author on Polycount: 'the vertex normal version cannot achieve the same quality because you need to take multiple samples of the input at different locations to get good curvature, and this is not possible without sampling a texture.' (polycount.com/discussion/202689). Multi-sample normal-MAP texture reads are required instead.

CORRECTION to research_corpus/materials/dust_accumulation_mask_procedural.md Reference 3: its citation 'Real-Time Procedural Texture Synthesis -- GPU Gems 3' does NOT exist as a real chapter title -- independently checked against NVIDIA's own GPU Gems index (developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/...) and web search; no such chapter is found in GPU Gems 3 or any volume. The real, closest on-topic chapter is GPU Gems 2, Chapter 26, 'Implementing Improved Perlin Noise' (Simon Green, NVIDIA), independently confirmed by WebFetch this session. This is a second confabulated-citation incident in this project's research corpus (cf. the 'NASA TR 1967-304' precedent) -- caught here by independent verification rather than trusting the corpus file, per this project's explicit don't-trust-prior-claims culture.

CORRECTION to the same corpus file's Reference 2: it attributes specific numeric thresholds (normal.z < -0.3 -> 0.8x, |normal.z| > 0.8 -> 1.0x, normal.z > 0.3 -> 0.0x) to 'Unreal Engine 5 Material Editor Documentation'. Independently re-fetching Epic's actual current Vector Material Expressions documentation shows NO such threshold constants anywhere in the node reference text -- these numbers are not sourced from official docs as claimed and must be treated as an unverified starting guess, not a documented engine fact.

nodes.reality: The original caveat (wrong pawn class DefaultPawn + unregistered MCP actions) does NOT reproduce now: fresh sleepwalk (simtest_c18e964f43800746) and direct PIE inspection both show BP_Astronaut_Character_C correctly possessed throughout; interact/drop actions were already registered in sleepwalker.py's _do_action by a prior commit (0ae87c4). But 4/9 beats still failed, and none of Bend/PickUp/Drop/Shovel actually function: chimeradefaultlevel's active GameMode (ADeepSpaceTraderGameMode, per Config/DefaultGame.ini GlobalDefaultGameMode, confirmed via the level's own .umap binary string search) never sets PlayerControllerClass, so it silently falls back to the input-less base APlayerController. The only class that binds ANY on-foot input (ADemoPlayerController: Move/Turn/LookUp/Jump via legacy AxisMappings in Config/DefaultInput.ini) is paired with a DIFFERENT, currently-unused GameMode (ADemoOnFootGameMode). Proven experimentally in a clean single-MCP-connection session: W held 2s -> CharMoveComp Velocity stays [0,0,0], zero displacement; Space (Jump) -> zero Z-change, no MOVE_Falling transition. This is task_c11196d2 (regolith_yard movement regression, 'pawn frozen at spawn'), now root-caused precisely instead of merely suspected -- and it also explains the verb_interactions spatial-beat failures. SEPARATELY, even once movement is fixed, Bend/PickUp/Drop still have NO input path at all: ADemoPlayerController never binds Interact/Drop/Crouch actions (only Move/Turn/LookUp/Jump), UPickupInteractionComponent is not attached to BP_Astronaut_Character_C (confirmed via 2 independent component listings: get_actor_details AND get_components both show exactly 5 components, none of them a pickup/interaction component), and no APickupActor exists anywhere in the level to pick up (Prop_Weapon, the only weapon-like actor, is a plain decorative StaticMeshActor). ATool_Shovel has no Dig()/Shovel() function at all -- static mesh + numeric metadata only. The beats' shallow expects (is_pie + pawn_class only, no functional state check) mask all of this: 5/9 beats 'reached' on the fresh sleepwalk despite zero of the 5 target verbs actually functioning end-to-end.
nodes.lesson_hint: Verb-interaction (and likely other on-foot) beat scripts need functional-state expects (velocity/displacement, capsule half-height, inventory count, actor-destroyed/spawned) not just is_pie+pawn_class -- shallow position/class checks pass even when the entire input pipeline is dead. DeepSpaceTraderGameMode.cpp is generator-owned (core/game_code_generator.py) -- the real fix (PlayerControllerClass = ADemoPlayerController, or equivalent) belongs in the generator template, not a hand-edit, and should be coordinated since other concurrent sessions actively depend on this GameMode's DemoTerminal/station/economy spawning.

nodes.error_message: CONFIRMED BUG: passing 'location' directly to manage_geometry create_* bakes the offset into the generated mesh's LOCAL vertex data AND sets the actor's Transform.Location to the same value, so the rendered mesh ends up at 2x the requested world position (e.g. requested z=1400 -> rendered at z=2800, confirmed via get_actor_bounds on 2 independent actors, cylinder and cone). WORKAROUND: never pass 'location' to create_*; spawn with no location (renders at local/world 0,0,0), then use a SEPARATE control_actor set_transform call to move it. This matches (and explains) why MCP_PATHWAYS.md pathway #14's documented recipe already used this 2-step pattern.

nodes.error_message: CONFIRMED BUG: the 'radius' parameter is not applied to create_cone's generated mesh -- requesting radius=200 AND radius=800 both produced identical extent.x=extent.y=50 (confirmed via get_actor_bounds, 2 independent clean spawns with different radius values, one uncontaminated by the concurrent-PIE issue below). 'height' is correctly applied (extent.z = height/2 both times). WORKAROUND: spawn the cone, read its bounds, then apply a corrective non-uniform control_actor set_transform scale (scale.x=scale.y=target_radius/50, scale.z=1.0) to reach the intended radius without distorting height. Cone's default orientation is apex-up (no rotation needed) when built pointing +Z, confirmed visually.

nodes.context: Re-ran docs/beats/verb_interactions.beats.json fresh (2 sessions) now that task_c11196d2's input-binding fix is verified live; expected the 5 previously-untested-under-real-movement position beats (shovel x3, visor, weapon) to now cleanly reach since W finally produces real displacement.
nodes.expectation: Beats reach cleanly now that input works, or fail with evidence indicting the verb itself.
nodes.reality: All 5 fail on real, reproducible forward drift, NOT a verb defect: pawn x climbed 9535->19929uu (session 1, simtest_fadc939050ee23a7) and 9526->19728uu (session 2, simtest_e9854be8cf3d0d83) while y stayed pinned at spawn's 400 both times -- proof of genuine, working W-movement, not noise. Root cause: the beats run sequentially in one continuous PIE session with no position reset between them, and the level's actual spawn (Player_Astronaut at 3200,400,130, left there by an unrelated prior session's sand-footstep testing, never restored) is nowhere near the original walk-forward-through-pads choreography's assumption (Pad_Metal(0,0)->Pad_Rock(2000,0)->Pad_Sand(4000,0)). Attempted fix: move_to teleport (BugItGo) to each beat's own pawn_within target before its hold -- reverted, BugItGo is hard-rejected during active PIE (see pathway bugitgo_pie above). actor_exists checks (SandDrift_FX, Display_Suit) passed cleanly both sessions regardless of drift, confirming those actors genuinely exist at their documented locations -- only the pawn_within reachability check is broken by the rig, not the level content.
nodes.lesson_hint: A beat file authored/calibrated while movement was dead can carry position assumptions that were never truly exercised; fixing an upstream input bug can retroactively expose latent rig-choreography bugs in beats that previously 'passed' only because the pawn never moved. Position-dependent beats should either reset position explicitly at the start of each beat or avoid absolute-coordinate assumptions.

nodes.reality: Chimera.log lines 15290-15313 show the access violation callstacks are entirely inside UbaCli.exe (Unreal Build Accelerator's local execution helper) + KERNEL32/ntdll -- zero compiler diagnostic text, zero reference to DemoPlayerController anywhere. TWO independent UbaCli invocations (04:38:44 and 04:38:47) crashed identically, ending in 'Reload/Re-instancing Complete: No object changes detected' -- Live Coding never got a compiled patch to apply. A subsequent cold, synchronous UBT build of the IDENTICAL source (via core.ubt_builder.UBTBuilder, also using the UBA local executor) compiled DemoPlayerController.cpp with zero errors and zero warnings in 78.65s. This conclusively proves the new C++ was never the problem -- it was a UBA/Live-Coding-pathway tooling flake, not a source-code defect.

nodes.expectation: Given pathway #30 only flagged header changes as 'widely known to be unreliable-to-impossible' (empirical/probabilistic framing), there was a chance a small property addition might patch through, or fail ambiguously.
nodes.reality: LiveCoding failed cleanly and empirically for this exact diff: 'Reload/Re-instancing Complete: No object changes detected' followed by 'Live coding failed'. The editor process survived intact (same PID, Responding=True) -- a safe, non-corrupting failure, unlike the earlier UbaCli.exe access-violation pattern from tonight's crouch session. Root cause: this diff adds new UPROPERTY members (bIsHoldingItem, HeldItemName on UPickupInteractionComponent; PickupInteraction, bDemoPickupSpawned on ADemoPlayerController), a new ADemoPlayerController() constructor, and changes TryInteract()'s return type from void to bool -- real header/reflection-layout changes. UE5 Live Coding patches function bodies only; it does not re-run UnrealHeaderTool, so new UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION additions or layout changes cannot be hot-applied. This confirms (not just documents from precedent) MCP_PATHWAYS.md pathway #30's caveat as a hard, categorical limitation for this class of change, not just empirical flakiness.
nodes.lesson_hint: Any diff adding a new UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION/constructor to a UCLASS should skip LiveCoding.Compile entirely and go straight to flagging the cold-build requirement -- attempting it wastes ~20s but is safe (no corruption observed) and produces a clean, checkable failure signature ('No object changes detected' + 'Live coding failed') worth grep-ing for before assuming a crash.

nodes.context: Verb_Bend crouch was recorded 'verified' by a prior sleepwalker run whose beat checked pawn_z_below:90 — a proxy the LIVE bug also satisfied (capsule permanently shrunk at possess + gravity fall after reset).
nodes.expectation: A feature marked 'verified' on a sleepwalker sim should actually work in-engine.
nodes.reality: Root cause: ConfigureCrouchCapsule read GetUnscaledCapsuleRadius as a 'half height', called SetCapsuleSize on the STANDING capsule at possess, and never set NavAgentProps.bCanCrouch or SetCrouchedHalfHeight, so ACharacter::Crouch() was a no-op. Rewrote to the real engine API; verified by a REVERSIBLE hard-fact transition (CapsuleHalfHeight 90->40->90, Z 102->52->102) driven by real C input.
nodes.lesson_hint: Verify a state-TOGGLE feature by its reversible transition (down-on-press, up-on-release), read as a hard engine fact (component property), never an absolute-threshold proxy a static bug can satisfy.

nodes.context: Ground_Sand_Footprints was needs_refinement after 3 attempts; the study guide blamed blend-space notify propagation.
nodes.expectation: Footprint code that COMPILES means the feature runs.
nodes.reality: TWO deeper causes: (1) ALL prior footprint code was DEAD on the demo pawn - the anim-notify path never propagates through BS_Idle_Walk_Run, and ChimeraMovementComponent (SpawnFootprintDecal placeholder + dust/servo) is never installed on BP_Astronaut_Character (no CreateDefaultSubobject anywhere; the pawn runs stock CharMoveComp). (2) A fresh movement-driven UFootprintComponent worked, but hard-fact COUNT verification caught a frame-rate-dependence bug (one-print-per-tick undercounted to 0.42x at low fps); a per-step interpolation loop fixed it to 0.99x.
nodes.lesson_hint: Before extending a stuck feature, confirm the code that exists is the code that RUNS on the live pawn (FindComponentByClass on the actual PIE pawn) - a compiled component installed on nothing is dead. And verify count/RATE as a hard fact, not mere presence: it exposes frame-rate-dependent spawners a presence check would pass.

nodes.context: Wrote a fitness objective for a creature (height x base x margin) and expected the optimiser to find a quadruped
nodes.reality: It found a LOLLIPOP - a boulder on a pole over a tripod - in 3 seconds. Mass goes as r^2 and parsimony was charged per BONE, so one enormous bone was free. A degenerate winner is not a failure: it is the optimiser AUDITING THE SPEC at 35kHz and finding a hole I would have defended in code review. THE EXPLOIT IS THE PRODUCT.

nodes.context: Read 'best 1.0000' for 700 generations of training and concluded the search had CONVERGED
nodes.reality: It had not converged - it was FINISHED. Score is a weighted geometric mean of satisfactions each capped at 1.0, so once every constraint reads sat=1.00 there is NO GRADIENT LEFT TO CLIMB. A spec made only of BOUNDS gets you exactly the bounds - a minimally-compliant satisficer. Every objective needs at least one maximize term. Adding one took tip_deg from 22.04 (riding its min of 22) to 31.53.

nodes.context: Evolved walker scored 13.52 body lengths under pybullet single-rollout evaluation; treated as a strong gait and staged for observation
nodes.reality: It was chaos, not a gait: gait.py periodicity 0.25 (no cycle), a 1-micron start-height nudge cost 5.5 body lengths, and it scored 2.41 (worse than untrained) under honest 16-restart evaluation. One rollout from one start is a coin toss, not a measurement. Root cause: TORQUE 35 N.m/kg (10x a human hip) flung the body 3.4 km up; pybullet's constraint solver contained the violence instead of NaN-ing, so it lived permanently in the ballistic regime with no contact to form a limit cycle. Fixed by moving to mujoco-warp on GPU (33.7x), scoring worst-of-16 randomized restarts, and correcting the actuators; first honest winner reached periodicity 0.78, robustness 0.76 (a robust rhythmic crawl).

nodes.context: tb-0168 Substrate rung A+B: brick->splat emission + gait coherence, scoring splat-vs-mesh render quality with a first-cut frame-to-frame pixel-delta ratio (splat vs marching-cubes mesh render of the same limb, same lights)
nodes.expectation: a ratio > 2.0x (my own initial kill bar) at a single sampling density would mean 'relighting artifacts dominate' / 'splats shear-swim-pop', i.e. a KILL for both rungs A and B
nodes.reality: single-density ratios WERE elevated (2.53x light-sweep, 3.17x gait) crossing my own kill bar, but a stability check (same ratio recomputed at 2x and 4x the sampling density: N=[6,12,24] light steps, N=[6,12,18] gait frames) showed the ratio essentially CONSTANT (max/min 1.03 and 1.04) plus exact determinism (repeat-render MAE=0.0) -- the signature of a smooth, proportional higher-gain shading response (per-voxel normals are noisier than pooled marching-cubes normals), not instability. The direct structural test (rigidity_cv, k=6 neighbour-distance CV across the trained gait) confirmed no shear: ratio 1.22, stable across N too. Both rungs SURVIVE once the ratio is stability-checked instead of trusted at one sample.
nodes.lesson_hint: a single-sample frame-to-frame delta ratio cannot distinguish 'stable higher-gain response' from 'genuine instability/artifacts' -- rerun the same ratio at 2x/4x the sampling density (light steps or gait frames); a stable ratio (max/min near 1.0) plus a determinism check (identical inputs twice -> 0 delta) is required before calling an elevated ratio a KILL. This is TRAINING_PROTOCOL.md SS3.5's 'one rollout is a coin toss' lesson applied to a rendering comparison instead of a gait rollout.
